headline: Today in Tech & Research
narrative_html:
Today's Technical Digest: May 6, 2024

These articles collectively highlight the rapid evolution of AI tools, infrastructure, and protocols, alongside clever hardware hacking and deep dives into information theory. The most concerning trend is the apparent rush to standardize agent protocols without sufficient engineering discipline, which could lead to significant technical debt as these systems mature.

CodeLLMs and Text-to-SQL Innovations

Two papers caught my eye today about the evolving landscape of AI code generation and database interaction.

The first paper on benchmarking CodeLLMs and agents reveals a significant imbalance in how we're evaluating these systems. While we're obsessively benchmarking code generation (60% of benchmarks!), we're almost completely ignoring requirements engineering (5%) and design phases (3%). This mirrors the industry's fixation on "code generation" rather than the full software development lifecycle. If we want AI to truly transform software engineering, we need to develop benchmarks that test the entire process, not just Python code synthesis.

The second paper, HEXGEN-TEXT2SQL, tackles a practical problem: how do you efficiently schedule and execute multi-stage LLM workflows for Text-to-SQL systems on GPU clusters? Their hierarchical scheduling approach claims impressive improvements - 1.41× faster latency and 1.65× better throughput compared to vLLM. This is the unglamorous but critical infrastructure work that will determine whether these LLM-based systems can actually perform in production environments. Worth investigating if you're building systems that require coordinating multiple LLM calls with interdependencies.

DIY Hardware Hacking

The PCB Strain Gauge project is a delightful bit of hardware ingenuity. The creator built a strain gauge where the PCB itself is the sensing element, capable of measuring deflections in the micrometer range. This is a clever approach that simplifies construction while maintaining sensitivity. The project includes full manufacturing specs, assembly instructions, and even sample firmware. If you're into electronics or IoT sensing, this could be an elegant solution for mechanical sensing applications.

Bioinformatics and Information Theory

The article on DNA information content is a fascinating exploration of information theory applied to biology. The author dives into the nuances of different definitions of "information" - storage space, Kolmogorov complexity, and Shannon information - and how each gives a different answer to the question "how much information is in DNA?"

What makes this piece exceptional is how it tackles the philosophical and mathematical challenges of quantifying biological information. The compression angle is particularly interesting - depending on your approach, human DNA might compress by either 25% or 99%, reflecting different notions of what constitutes "information." This piece rewards a full read, especially if you're interested in the intersection of information theory and biology.

Software Engineering Improvements

The Adaptive Hashing article describes SBCL's (Steel Bank Common Lisp) approach to making hash tables both faster and more robust. Rather than using a single hash function, they adaptively switch between different hashing strategies based on the actual keys being stored. For EQ hash tables, they start with a constant hash function for small tables, then progressively upgrade to more sophisticated hash functions as needed. For EQUAL hash tables with composite keys, they initially hash only portions of the keys and expand as collisions increase.

This pragmatic approach balances performance in common cases with robustness against pathological inputs. The results show meaningful improvements in both aspects, and the technique could be applicable in other languages and systems.

Protocol Design Critique

The critical analysis of MCP (Model Context Protocol) raises serious concerns about the design of this emerging standard for LLM/agent interaction. The author argues that the HTTP transport methods (HTTP+SSE and "Streamable HTTP") are fundamentally flawed attempts to reinvent WebSockets. They point out poor documentation, confusing specifications, and questionable design decisions that suggest the protocol was rushed without proper engineering rigor.

This is a must-read if you're considering implementing MCP. The critique is technical and substantive, not just complaining. The author makes a compelling case that the current approach should be reconsidered in favor of WebSockets for HTTP transport. Given that major players like IBM and Google are releasing competing standards (ACP and A2A), we may be heading toward a messy period of competing protocols before consolidation occurs.

item.title: Software Development Life Cycle Perspective: A Survey of Benchmarks for CodeLLMs and Agents
item.summary:
Code large language models (CodeLLMs) and agents have shown great promise in
tackling complex software engineering tasks.Compared to traditional software
engineering methods, CodeLLMs and agents offer stronger abilities, and can
flexibly process inputs and outputs in both natural and code. Benchmarking
plays a crucial role in evaluating the capabilities of CodeLLMs and agents,
guiding their development and deployment. However, despite their growing
significance, there remains a lack of comprehensive reviews of benchmarks for
CodeLLMs and agents. To bridge this gap, this paper provides a comprehensive
review of existing benchmarks for CodeLLMs and agents, studying and analyzing
181 benchmarks from 461 relevant papers, covering the different phases of the
software development life cycle (SDLC). Our findings reveal a notable imbalance
in the coverage of current benchmarks, with approximately 60% focused on the
software development phase in SDLC, while requirements engineering and software
design phases receive minimal attention at only 5% and 3%, respectively.
Additionally, Python emerges as the dominant programming language across the
reviewed benchmarks. Finally, this paper highlights the challenges of current
research and proposes future directions, aiming to narrow the gap between the
theoretical capabilities of CodeLLMs and agents and their application in
real-world scenarios.

items.why:
Given your background—deep technical fluency, experience with both research and product development, and a current focus on building practical LLM-backed tools—the paper you mention is likely to be of moderate, but not transformative, value to you. The survey appears to be a comprehensive catalog of benchmarks for CodeLLMs and agents, with a focus on how these benchmarks map onto different phases of the software development life cycle (SDLC). If your immediate goal is to get a broad, structured overview of the current landscape of CodeLLM evaluation—what’s being measured, where the gaps are, and what languages and tasks are over- or under-represented—this paper will give you a solid, up-to-date reference.

However, it doesn’t sound like the paper is breaking new ground in terms of methodology, nor is it likely to contain actionable insights for building novel products or tools on top of LLMs. Its main contribution is mapping the territory: what’s been benchmarked, what hasn’t, and where the field is lopsided. For someone building LLM-powered developer tools or agent systems, this could help you identify underexplored areas (e.g., requirements engineering or design tasks) that might be ripe for innovation, or at least alert you to where the “herd” is currently focused (Python, coding tasks, etc.). But if you’re already tracking the major benchmarks and have a sense of where LLMs are strong or weak, this might feel like a confirmation rather than a revelation.

In short: this paper is a useful meta-resource if you want to quickly orient yourself in the CodeLLM/agent benchmarking space, especially if you’re considering targeting less-served parts of the SDLC with your products. But if you’re looking for deep technical insight, new evaluation paradigms, or product inspiration beyond “here’s what’s been benchmarked so far,” it may not be essential reading. Skim the intro, tables, and discussion for gaps and future directions; if nothing jumps out as directly relevant to your plans, you can probably move on without FOMO.
items.overview:
This paper presents a comprehensive review of benchmarks used to evaluate code large language models (CodeLLMs) and agents, with a particular focus on how these benchmarks correspond to the various phases of the software development life cycle (SDLC). The authors analyze 181 benchmarks drawn from 461 relevant papers, systematically categorizing them according to their alignment with SDLC phases such as requirements engineering, software design, and software development. The review reveals a pronounced imbalance in benchmark coverage: approximately 60% of benchmarks are concentrated on the software development phase, while requirements engineering and software design are significantly underrepresented, accounting for only 5% and 3% of benchmarks, respectively. Additionally, the analysis finds that Python is the dominant programming language across these benchmarks.

The paper's primary contribution is its structured mapping of the current benchmarking landscape for CodeLLMs and agents. By cataloging what has been benchmarked and identifying areas that lack sufficient evaluation, the survey provides a clear overview of both the strengths and gaps in current research. For practitioners and researchers, this mapping can be used to quickly orient themselves within the field, understand which tasks and languages have received the most attention, and identify underexplored areas—such as requirements engineering and design tasks—that may warrant further investigation or innovation. The survey also discusses challenges in current research and suggests directions for future work, with the aim of narrowing the gap between the theoretical capabilities of CodeLLMs and agents and their practical deployment in real-world software engineering scenarios.

While the paper does not introduce new methodologies or propose novel evaluation paradigms, it serves as a useful meta-resource for those seeking an up-to-date reference on CodeLLM and agent benchmarks. Its value lies in providing a consolidated view of the field, which can inform decisions about where to focus development efforts, especially for those interested in building LLM-powered developer tools or agent systems. However, for readers who are already familiar with the major benchmarks and the general distribution of research efforts, the paper may function more as a confirmation of existing knowledge rather than a source of new technical insights or product ideas.
items.context: CodeLLMs (code-focused large language models) and agents are AI systems designed to assist with or automate software development tasks, such as code generation, bug fixing, or documentation. Benchmarks are standardized tests or datasets used to evaluate how well these models perform on specific tasks. The Software Development Life Cycle (SDLC) refers to the stages involved in creating software, typically including requirements gathering, design, implementation (coding), testing, deployment, and maintenance. This paper surveys existing benchmarks for CodeLLMs and agents, organizing them according to which SDLC phase they target, and highlights which tasks, programming languages, or SDLC stages are well-covered or neglected in current evaluations. This helps researchers and practitioners understand the current state of CodeLLM assessment, spot gaps in coverage (such as few benchmarks for early-stage design or requirements tasks), and identify opportunities for future work or product development.

item.title: HEXGEN-TEXT2SQL: Optimizing LLM Inference Request Scheduling for Agentic Text-to-SQL Workflow
item.summary:
Recent advances in leveraging the agentic paradigm of large language models
(LLMs) utilization have significantly enhanced Text-to-SQL capabilities,
enabling users without specialized database expertise to query data
intuitively. However, deploying these agentic LLM-based Text-to-SQL systems in
production poses substantial challenges due to their inherently multi-stage
workflows, stringent latency constraints, and potentially heterogeneous GPU
infrastructure in enterprise environments. Current LLM serving frameworks lack
effective mechanisms for handling interdependent inference tasks, dynamic
latency variability, and resource heterogeneity, leading to suboptimal
performance and frequent service-level objective (SLO) violations. In this
paper, we introduce HEXGEN-TEXT2SQL, a novel framework designed explicitly to
schedule and execute agentic multi-stage LLM-based Text-to-SQL workflows on
heterogeneous GPU clusters that handle multi-tenant end-to-end queries.
HEXGEN-TEXT2SQL introduce a hierarchical scheduling approach combining global
workload-balanced task dispatching and local adaptive urgency-guided
prioritization, guided by a systematic analysis of agentic Text-to-SQL
workflows. Additionally, we propose a lightweight simulation-based method for
tuning critical scheduling hyperparameters, further enhancing robustness and
adaptability. Our extensive evaluation on realistic Text-to-SQL benchmarks
demonstrates that HEXGEN-TEXT2SQL significantly outperforms state-of-the-art
LLM serving frameworks. Specifically, HEXGEN-TEXT2SQL reduces latency deadlines
by up to 1.67$\times$ (average: 1.41$\times$) and improves system throughput by
up to 1.75$\times$ (average: 1.65$\times$) compared to vLLM under diverse,
realistic workload conditions. Our code is available at
https://github.com/Relaxed-System-Lab/Hexgen-Flow.

items.overview:
HEXGEN-TEXT2SQL is a framework designed to address the challenges of deploying agentic, multi-stage large language model (LLM) Text-to-SQL workflows in production environments. These workflows enable users without specialized database knowledge to query data using natural language, but their deployment is complicated by factors such as interdependent inference tasks, strict latency requirements, and the use of heterogeneous GPU resources in enterprise settings. Existing LLM serving frameworks are not equipped to handle these complexities, often resulting in inefficient resource utilization and frequent violations of service-level objectives (SLOs).

The core contribution of HEXGEN-TEXT2SQL is a hierarchical scheduling mechanism tailored for agentic Text-to-SQL workflows operating on heterogeneous GPU clusters. This approach combines global workload-balanced task dispatching with local, adaptive urgency-guided prioritization, informed by a systematic analysis of the unique characteristics of agentic workflows. Additionally, the framework introduces a lightweight, simulation-based method for tuning scheduling hyperparameters, which enhances the system’s robustness and adaptability to changing workloads and resource availability. The framework is evaluated on realistic Text-to-SQL benchmarks, where it demonstrates significant improvements over state-of-the-art LLM serving systems such as vLLM, reducing latency deadlines by up to 1.67× (average 1.41×) and increasing system throughput by up to 1.75× (average 1.65×) under diverse workload conditions.

The significance of HEXGEN-TEXT2SQL lies in its focus on the infrastructure and scheduling challenges associated with complex, agentic LLM workflows, rather than on LLM model development itself. For practitioners and researchers working on LLM tooling, workflow orchestration, or composable systems, the framework addresses a critical bottleneck in efficiently managing multi-stage, interdependent LLM calls under real-world constraints. The open-sourcing of HEXGEN-TEXT2SQL further increases its practical utility, providing a resource for those building or contributing to the next generation of LLM-backed products and tools. The framework’s advances in hierarchical scheduling and simulation-based tuning represent a substantial step forward in the management of agentic LLM workflows on heterogeneous hardware.
items.context: HEXGEN-TEXT2SQL addresses a key challenge in deploying agentic (multi-step, decision-making) large language model (LLM) systems for tasks like converting natural language to SQL queries (Text-to-SQL). In these workflows, multiple LLM calls—often with dependencies between them—must be scheduled efficiently to minimize latency and maximize hardware utilization, especially when resources are limited. Existing LLM infrastructure (like vLLM or Ray Serve) typically focuses on single, independent inference requests and struggles with orchestrating complex, interdependent workflows across heterogeneous hardware. This paper introduces a hierarchical scheduling framework and simulation-based tuning to optimize how LLM inference requests are managed in such agentic pipelines, making it easier to build robust, production-grade LLM applications that require more than just single-shot prompting.

item.title: Strain gauge made out of PCB
item.summary: PCB Strain Gauge A strain gauge, with amplifier, where the sensing element is the circuit board itself. Sensitive enough to measure deflections in the range of micrometers while having a full scale deflection range of +/- 3cm. strain_demo.mp4 View files with KiCanvas! Manufacturing The recommended board thickness is 0.6mm, although it could be made thicker or thinner for different applications. Thinner boards will result in a smaller output voltage swing. strain_gauge_3.zip 20 mm x 118 mm, 2 layer 0.15mm (~6mil) min trace width 4-element sensing bridge strain_gauge_3_rotated.zip Same as the previous one, except it uses 2-element sensing. Lower thermal drift and bias from manufacturing (theoretically) stran_gauge_stiffener.zip 20 mm x 42 mm rectangle to keep the component side from flexing Can be affixed to the board with 3M VHB 5906 Assembly This project was made with hand-assembly in mind, and does not require hot air or a reflow oven. The board can be used standalone with an integrated microcontroller (Seeed Studio XIAO RP2040) or an external microcontroller through the header pins. The external ADC (U5) can be omitted, and the analog voltage can be sampled directly on the "OUT" pin. The bias voltage generator (U8, U4) can also be omitted by placing a jumper wire between pins 2&3 on U8. Doing this will result in a measureable voltage on the output when no force is applied. Programming The included sample firmware will wait until a serial console is opened, perform a 5 second offset calibration, then sample continuously at the lowest gain setting. The graph.py script can be used to display the output. For high sensitivity measurements, it's important to let the board reach a stable operating temperature for at least 5 minutes before calibrating. Customatization To customize the shape of the sensing element, draw_footprint.ipynb can be used to generate an outline of a given width, height and curvature. The resulting .svg can be imported into Inkscape and converted into a KiCad footprint using the svg2shenzen tool.

items.overview:
The "PCB strain gauge" project presents a method for constructing a strain gauge in which the printed circuit board (PCB) itself serves as the sensing element. This device is capable of detecting deflections in the micrometer range, with a full-scale deflection capacity of +/- 3 cm. The recommended board thickness is 0.6 mm, but this can be adjusted for specific applications, with thinner boards producing smaller output voltage swings. The standard design uses a 20 mm x 118 mm, two-layer PCB with a minimum trace width of 0.15 mm (approximately 6 mil), and incorporates a 4-element sensing bridge. An alternative version uses a 2-element bridge, which theoretically offers lower thermal drift and reduced manufacturing bias. A stiffener, measuring 20 mm x 42 mm, can be affixed to the component side of the board using 3M VHB 5906 tape to prevent unwanted flexing.

Assembly of the strain gauge is designed for hand-soldering and does not require specialized equipment such as a reflow oven or hot air tools. The board can function either as a standalone device—using an integrated microcontroller like the Seeed Studio XIAO RP2040—or be interfaced with an external microcontroller via header pins. The design allows for the omission of the external ADC (U5), enabling direct sampling of the analog voltage from the "OUT" pin, and the bias voltage generator (U8, U4) can be bypassed by connecting pins 2 and 3 on U8, though this results in a measurable voltage at rest. The provided firmware supports a 5-second offset calibration upon serial connection and samples continuously at the lowest gain setting. For data visualization, a Python script ("graph.py") is included. Accurate, high-sensitivity measurements require the board to reach thermal equilibrium for at least five minutes prior to calibration.

Customization is supported through the "draw_footprint.ipynb" tool, which generates outlines for sensing elements with specified dimensions and curvature. These can be exported as SVG files, edited in Inkscape, and converted into KiCad footprints using the svg2shenzen tool. The project is fully documented and includes open source design files, making it accessible for modification and integration into other systems. This approach demonstrates a way to extend standard PCB manufacturing and assembly processes to create precision sensors, which may have implications for rapid prototyping, hardware-software integration, and scalable sensing applications. The project serves as an example of how open, well-documented hardware tools can provide foundational building blocks for new product development and experimentation.
items.context: A strain gauge is a sensor that measures the amount of deformation (strain) in an object when a force is applied, typically used in engineering to detect loads, pressure, or structural stress. Traditionally, strain gauges are made from thin metal foils or wires, but the 'PCB strain gauge' project innovatively uses the copper traces on a standard printed circuit board (PCB) as the sensing element. By designing specific patterns in the PCB's copper layers, the board itself can flex slightly under force, causing measurable changes in electrical resistance that can be read by simple electronics. This approach leverages common, low-cost PCB manufacturing processes, making it accessible for rapid prototyping and integration into custom hardware. For software engineers, this means it's now possible to build devices that sense physical forces without specialized hardware, opening up new opportunities for hardware-software integration, IoT projects, and experimentation with real-world data inputs.

item.title: How much information is in DNA?
item.summary: https://press.asimov.com/articles/dna-informationThis is an article that just appeared in Asimov Press, who kindly agreed that I could publish it here and also humored my deep emotional need to use words like “Sparklepuff”.Do you like information theory? Do you like molecular biology? Do you like the idea of smashing them together and seeing what happens? If so, then here’s a question: How much information is in your DNA?When I first looked into this question, I thought it was simple:Human DNA has about 3.1 billion base pairs.Each base pair can take one of four values (A, T, C, or G)It takes 2 bits to encode one of four possible values (00, 01, 10, or 11)Thus, human DNA contains 6.2 billion bits.Easy, right? Sure, except:You have two versions of each base pair, one from each of your parents. Should you count both?All humans have almost identical DNA. Does that matter?DNA can be compressed. Should you look at the compressed representation?It’s not clear how much of our DNA actually does something useful. The insides of your cells are a convulsing pandemonium of interacting “hacks”, designed to keep working even as mutations constantly screw around with the DNA itself. Should we only count the “useful” parts?Such questions quickly run into the limits of knowledge for both biology and computer science. To answer them, we need to figure out what exactly we mean by “information” and how that’s related to what’s happening inside cells. In attempting that, I will lead you through a frantic tour of information theory and molecular biology. We’ll meet some strange characters, including genomic compression algorithms based on deep learning, retrotransposons, and Kolmogorov complexity.Ultimately, I’ll argue that the intuitive idea of information in a genome is best captured by a new definition of a “bit”—one that’s unknowable with our current level of scientific knowledge.What is “information”? This isn’t just a pedantic question, as there are actually several different mathematical definitions of a “bit”. Often, the differences don’t matter, but for DNA, they turn out to matter a lot, so let’s start with the simplest.In the storage space definition, a bit is a “slot” in which you can store one of two possible values. If some object can represent 2ⁿ possible patterns, then it contains n bits, regardless of which pattern actually happens to be stored.So here’s a question we can answer precisely: How much information could your DNA store?A few reminders: DNA is a polymer. It’s a long chain of chunks of ~40 atoms called “nucleotides”. There are four different chunks, commonly labeled A, T, C, and G. In humans, DNA comes in 23 pieces of different lengths, called “chromosomes”. Humans are “diploid”, meaning we have two versions of each chromosome. We get one from each of our parents, made by randomly weaving together sections from the two chromosomes they got from their parents. At least, that's true for the first 22 chromosomes. For the last, females have two "X" chromosomes, while males have one "X" and one "Y" chromosome. There's no mixing between these, so men pass on one to their children pretty much unchanged1.Chromosomes 1-22 have a total of 2.875 billion nucleotides; the X chromosome has 156 million, and the Y chromosome has 62 million. From here, we can calculate the total storage space in your DNA. Remember, each nucleotide has 4 options, corresponding to 2 bits. So if you’re female, your total storage space is:(2×2875 + 2×156) million nucleotides× 2 bits / nucleotide= 12.12 billion bits= 1.51 GB.If you’re male, the total storage space is:(2×2875 + 156 + 62) million nucleotides× 2 bits / nucleotide= 11.94 billion bits= 1.49 GB.For comparison, a standard single-layer DVD can store 37.6 billion bits or 4.7 GB. The code for your body, magnificent as it is, takes up as much space as around 40 minutes of standard definition video.So in principle, your DNA could represent around 212,000,000,000 different patterns. But hold on. Given human common ancestry, the chromosome pair you got from your mother is almost identical to the one you got from your father. And even ignoring that, there are long sequences of nucleotides that are repeated over and over in your DNA, enough to make up a significant fraction of the total. It seems weird to count all this repeated stuff. So perhaps we want a more nuanced definition of “information.”A string of 12 billion zeros is much longer than this article. But most people would (I hope) agree that this article contains more information than a string of 12 billion zeros. Why?One of the fundamental ideas from information theory is to define information in terms of compression. Roughly speaking, the “information” in some string is the length of the shortest possible compressed representation of that string.So how much can you compress DNA? Answers to this question are all over the place. Some people claim it can be compressed by more than 99 percent, while others claim the state of the art is only around 25 percent. This discrepancy is explained by different definitions of “compression”, which turn out to correspond to different notions of “information”. If you pick any two random people on Earth, almost all of their DNA will be exactly the same. It's often said that people are 99.9 percent genetically identical, but this is wrong — it only measures substitutions and neglects things like insertions, deletions, and transpositions. If you account for all these things, the best estimate is that we are ~99.6 percent identical2.The fact that we share so much DNA is key to how some algorithms can compress DNA by more than 99 percent. They do this by first storing a reference genome, which includes all the DNA that’s shared by all people and perhaps the most common variants for regions of DNA where people differ. Then, for each individual person, these algorithms only store the differences from the reference genome. Because that reference only has to be stored once, it isn’t counted in the compressed representation.That’s great if you want to cram as many of your friends’ genomes on a hard drive as possible. But it’s a strange definition to use if you want to measure the “information content of DNA”. It implies that any genomic content that doesn’t change between individuals isn’t important enough to count as “information”. However, we know from evolutionary biology that it’s often the most crucial DNA that changes the least precisely because it’s so important. Heritability tends to be lower for genes more closely related to reproduction.The best compression without a reference seems to be around 25 percent. (I expect this number to rise a bit over time, as the newest methods use deep learning and research is ongoing.) That’s not a lot of compression. However, these algorithms are benchmarked in terms of how well they compress a genome that includes only one copy of each chromosome. Since your two chromosomes are almost identical (at least, ignoring the Y chromosome), I’d guess that you could represent the other half almost for free, meaning a compression rate of around 50 percent + ½ × 25 percent ≈ 62 percent.So if you compress DNA using an algorithm with a reference genome, it can be compressed by more than 99 percent, down to less than 120 million bits. But if you compress it without a reference genome, the best you can do is 62 percent, meaning 4.6 billion bits.Which of these is right? The answer is that either could be right. There are two different definitions of a “bit” in information theory that correspond to different types of compression.In the Kolmogorov complexity definition, named after the remarkable Soviet mathematician Andrey Kolmogorov, a bit is a property of a particular string of 1s and 0s. items.overview:
The article "How much information is in DNA?" examines the intersection of information theory and molecular biology by rigorously analyzing how to quantify the information content of human DNA. It begins with a straightforward calculation: human DNA consists of approximately 3.1 billion base pairs, each of which can be one of four nucleotides (A, T, C, or G), requiring 2 bits to encode. This yields a raw storage estimate of 6.2 billion bits per haploid genome. Taking into account human diploidy—two copies of each chromosome, one from each parent—the total rises to about 12.12 billion bits (1.51 GB) for females and 11.94 billion bits (1.49 GB) for males, considering the differing sizes of the X and Y chromosomes. For context, this is roughly equivalent to 40 minutes of standard definition video on a DVD.

However, the article quickly complicates this naive calculation by addressing several key issues: the high degree of similarity between parental chromosomes, the prevalence of repeated sequences in the genome, and the distinction between DNA that is functionally significant versus non-coding or repetitive regions. It introduces the concept of information as defined by compression, referencing both Kolmogorov complexity (the length of the shortest program that can reproduce a string) and Shannon information (probabilistic measures of uncertainty and entropy). The article discusses how DNA can be compressed using reference-based algorithms, which exploit the fact that humans are approximately 99.6% genetically identical when insertions, deletions, and transpositions are considered. With a reference genome, individual DNA can be compressed by over 99%, down to less than 120 million bits. Without a reference, the best current methods achieve about 25% compression on a single chromosome set, or roughly 62% when accounting for the diploid nature of human DNA, yielding a compressed size of about 4.6 billion bits.

These distinctions are not merely academic; they have practical implications for genomic data storage and for how we conceptualize "information" in biological systems. The article highlights that different definitions of a "bit"—whether based on storage capacity, compressibility, or functional content—lead to significantly different answers to the question of how much information DNA contains. This nuanced exploration is relevant beyond biology, as it mirrors challenges faced in fields such as software engineering, data compression, and artificial intelligence, where the meaning and measurement of information are also foundational concerns. The article's critical examination of assumptions, edge cases, and the practical impact of theoretical definitions provides a rigorous framework for understanding information in complex systems, and its approach offers a model for communicating intricate technical concepts clearly and precisely.
items.context: DNA, or deoxyribonucleic acid, is the molecule that encodes genetic instructions in living organisms, and its structure can be thought of as a long sequence of four chemical bases (A, T, C, G), analogous to a string of characters in software. Information theory, a mathematical framework developed by Claude Shannon, provides tools to quantify the amount of information in such sequences, often using concepts like entropy (a measure of unpredictability) and compression (how much a sequence can be reduced without losing meaning). Kolmogorov complexity, another key idea, measures the shortest possible description (algorithm or program) that can generate a given sequence, offering a way to think about the 'true' information content beyond just raw size. In genomics, these concepts help us understand not just how much data DNA holds, but also how efficiently it can be stored, transmitted, or analyzed—issues that overlap with challenges in software engineering, such as data compression, storage optimization, and algorithmic efficiency. Recent advances, including deep learning-based compression, are pushing the boundaries of how we handle massive genomic datasets, making this intersection of biology and information theory both practically and philosophically relevant to anyone interested in data, algorithms, or system design.

item.title: Adaptive Hashing
item.summary: Tags: tech, lisp, Date: 2025-05-02 At the 2024 ELS, I gave a talk on adaptive hashing, which focusses on making general purpose hash tables faster and more robust at the same time. Theory vs Practice Hash table theory most concerns itself with the asymptotic worst-case cost with a hash function chosen randomly from a family of hash functions. Although these results are very relevant in practice, those pesky constant factors, that the big-O cost ignores, do matter, and we don't pick hash functions randomly but fix the hash function for the lifetime of the hash table. There are Perfect Hashing algorithms, that choose an optimal hash function for a given set of keys. The drawback is that they either require the set of keys to be fixed or they are too slow to be used as general purpose hash tables. Still, the idea that we can do better by adapting the hash function to the actual keys is key. Can we do that online, that is, while the hash table is being used? Potential performance gains come from improving the constant factors mentioned above by having fewer collisions, and being more cache-friendly. The images above plot regret (the expected number of comparisons of per lookup minus the minimum achievable) and the measured run-time of PUT operations vs the number of keys in the hash table with a particular key distribution. Green is Murmur (a robust hash function), Blue is SBCL's expedient EQ hash. The wiggling of the graphs is due to the resizing of the hash table as keys are added to it. Note how SBCL's regret starts out much lower and becomes much higher than that of Murmur, but if anything, its advantage grows. Implementation The general idea is sound, but turning it into real performance gains is hard due to the cost of choosing a hash function and switching to it. First, we have to make some assumption about the distribution of keys. In fact, default hash functions in language runtimes often make such assumptions to make the common cases faster, usually at the cost of weakened worst-case guarantees. The rest of this post is about how SBCL's built-in hash tables, which had been reasonably fast, were modified. The core switching mechanism looks at the length of the collision chain on PUT operations, the collision count on rehash (when the hash table is grown), and the size of the hash table. Adapting EQ hash tables Init to to constant hash function. This a fancy way of saying that we do linear search in a vector internally. This is an EQ hash table, so key comparison is as single assembly instruction. When the hash table is grown to more than 32 keys and it must be rehashed anyway, we switch to a hash function that does a single right shift with the number of bits to shift determined from the longest common run of low-bits in the keys. If too many collisions, we switch to the previous default SBCL EQ-hash function that has been tuned for a long time. If too many collisions, we switch to Murmur, a general purpose hash. We could also go all the way to cryptographic hashes. In step 2, the hash function with the single shift fits the memory allocator's behaviour nicely: it is a perfect hash for keys forming arithmetic sequences, which is often approximately true for objects of the same type allocated in a loop. In this figure, the red line is the adaptive hash. Adapting EQUAL hash tables For composite keys, running the hash function is the main cost. Adaptive hashing does the following. For string keys, hash only the first and last 2 characters. For list keys, only hash the first 4 elements. If too many collisions, double the limit. So, SBCL hash tables have been adaptive for almost a year now, gaining some speed in common cases, and robustness in others. The full paper is here.

Finally, it’s a “tech deep cut” that’s likely to be underappreciated by the broader crowd but could be a conversation starter or a differentiator for you, especially if you’re building tools or libraries for other devs. Even if you don’t directly apply adaptive hashing, the mindset—questioning default assumptions, instrumenting for real-world usage, and adapting algorithms dynamically—maps well to the kind of product and infra work you’re aiming to do.

items.overview:
Adaptive hashing, as discussed in the referenced talk at the 2024 European Lisp Symposium, is an approach aimed at improving the speed and robustness of general-purpose hash tables by dynamically adjusting the hash function in use based on observed key patterns and collision behavior. Traditional hash table theory typically focuses on asymptotic worst-case costs under the assumption of randomly chosen hash functions, but in practice, constant factors and the fixed choice of hash function for the table's lifetime play a significant role in real-world performance. While perfect hashing algorithms exist for fixed key sets, they are generally impractical for mutable, general-purpose hash tables due to performance constraints. The adaptive hashing approach attempts to bridge this gap by monitoring the hash table's state during use—such as the length of collision chains, collision counts during rehashing, and table size—and switching hash functions when certain thresholds are met.

The implementation in SBCL’s built-in hash tables exemplifies this adaptive strategy. For EQ hash tables, the process begins with a constant hash function, effectively reducing to a linear search within a vector, leveraging the fact that key comparison is a single assembly instruction. When the table grows beyond 32 keys and a rehash is required, the system switches to a hash function that performs a single right shift, with the shift amount determined by the longest common run of low bits in the keys—this is particularly effective for keys that form arithmetic sequences, which is common for objects allocated in loops. If collision rates remain high, the system escalates to SBCL's long-standing default EQ hash function, and, if necessary, to the more robust Murmur hash function. For EQUAL hash tables, which handle composite keys, the adaptation involves initially hashing only the first and last two characters of strings or the first four elements of lists, doubling the limit if collisions persist. These changes have been in use in SBCL for nearly a year, yielding measurable performance improvements for common cases and increased robustness for less typical key distributions.

The significance of adaptive hashing extends beyond its immediate application in Lisp or SBCL. It addresses a practical gap between theoretical guarantees and the realities of production systems, where key distributions are rarely random and performance bottlenecks often arise from overlooked constant factors. The core technique—dynamically instrumenting and adapting algorithms based on real-world usage patterns—offers a generalizable strategy for systems and infrastructure design. This approach is relevant for anyone seeking to optimize runtime components, develop more resilient libraries, or build tools that respond effectively to diverse workloads. The adaptive hashing work demonstrates a concrete, deployed example of how algorithmic adaptivity can translate into tangible system-level gains.
items.context: Adaptive hashing is a technique used in hash table implementations where the system dynamically changes the hash function or internal data structures in response to observed patterns in the keys or collision rates during runtime. Traditional hash tables rely on a fixed hash function, which can lead to performance degradation if the input keys are not well-distributed or if adversarial patterns cause many collisions (multiple keys mapping to the same bucket). Adaptive hashing monitors the actual usage—such as the frequency and distribution of keys—and switches to alternative strategies (like different hash functions or even tree-based buckets) when it detects problematic patterns, thereby maintaining efficient lookups and inserts even in non-ideal, real-world scenarios. This approach bridges the gap between theoretical performance guarantees and the unpredictable nature of production workloads, making hash-based data structures more robust and performant.

item.title: A critical look at MCP
item.summary: TL;DR Background Protocol Transport Stdio HTTP+SSE / Streamable HTTP A Descent into Madness The Warning Signs... The Problem HTTP+SSE Mode "Streamable HTTP" Mode What Are the Implications for SSE Mode? What Are the Implications for "Streamable HTTP"? General implications Security Implications Authorization What Should Be Done Side note: Alternatives and Additions "MCP is an open protocol that standardizes how applications provide context to LLMs. Think of MCP like a USB-C port for AI applications. Just as USB-C provides a standardized way to connect your devices to various peripherals and accessories, MCP provides a standardized way to connect AI models to different data sources and tools." ― Anthropic TL;DR I would like for this to turn out to be a skill issue on my part, and hope that I'm missing something. During the past month,MCP (Model Context Protocol), which would enable LLMs to become agents and interact with the world, has really been blowing up. The idea is straightforward: let's standardize an API for LLM/Agents to interact with the world and how to inform the LLM/Agent about it. Things are moving really fast, and IBM recently released their own "orthogonal standard" to MCP called Agent Communication Protocol (ACP), followed closely by Google announcing Agent2Agent (A2A). MCP Servers and Clients are being built and published daily, and can be found at sites like mcp.so and pulsemcp.com. However, I'm astonished by the apparent lack of mature engineering practices. All the major players spend billions of dollars on training and tuning their models, only to turn around and, from what I can tell, have an interns write the documentation, providing subpar SDKs and very little in terms of implementation guidance. This trend seems to have continued with MCP, resulting in some very strange design decisions, poor documentation, and an even worse specification of the actual protocols. My conclusion is that the whole suggested setup for HTTP transport (SSE+HTTP and Streamable HTTP) should be thrown out and replaced with something that mimics stdio... Websockets. Background About three weeks ago, I decided to jump on the MCP bandwagon to give it a try and see how it could be used in our own environment. I'm very much a person who wants to understand how things actually work under the hood before I start using abstractions. Here we have a new protocol that works over different transports — how exciting! Anthropic is the company behind the MCP standardization effort, and MCP seems to be one of the major reasons Anthropic's CEO is thinking that most code will be written by LLMs within a year or so. The bet on coding tooling in particular seems to have been the guiding principle of the standardization effort based on how it feels to work with it. Protocol Simply put, it is a JSON-RPC protocol with predefined methods/endpoints designed to be used in conjunction with an LLM. This is not really the focus of this post, but there are things to be criticized about the protocol itself. Transport As with many applications post-2005, they're supposedly "local first" (ironically), and this seems to be very much the case with MCP. Looking at the transport protocol, you get a sense of where they're coming from—if their intention is to build LLM tools for coding on your laptop. They're probably looking at local IDEs (or more realistically, Cursor or Windsurf) and how to have the LLM interact with the local file system, databases, editors, language servers, and so on. There are essentially two main transport protocols (or three): stdio "Something over HTTP, the web seems to be a thing we probably should support." Stdio Using stdio essentially means starting a local MCP Server, hooking up stdout and stdin pipes from the server to the client, and starting to send JSON and using stderr for logging. It kind of breaks the Unix/Linux piping paradigm using these streams for bidirectional communication. When bidirectional communication is needed, we usually reach for a socket, unix socket or even a net socket. However, it is straightforward and easy to reason about, works out of the box in all OSes, no need to deal with sockets, and so on. So even if there is a critique to be made, I get it. HTTP+SSE / Streamable HTTP The HTTP transport is another story. There are two versions of the same mistake: HTTP+SSE (Server-Sent Events) transport, which is being replaced by "Streamable HTTP" (a made-up term) that uses REST semantics with SSE. But with a whole lot of extra confusion and corner cases on top. It can be summarized as: "Since we like SSE for LLM streaming, we're not using WebSockets. Instead, we're effectively implementing WebSockets on top of SSE and calling it 'Streamable HTTP' to make people think it's an accepted/known way of doing things." They discuss the problems with WebSockets (and the reason for Streamable HTTP) in this PR: modelcontextprotocol/pull/206, making some very strange contortions and straw-man arguments to not use WebSockets. At least one other person in the thread seems to agree with me: modelcontextprotocol/pull/206#issuecomment-2766559523. A Descent into Madness I set out to implement an MCP server in Golang. There isn't an official Go SDK, and I wanted to understand the protocol. This turned out to be a mistake for mental health... The Warning Signs... Looking at https://modelcontextprotocol.io, the documentation is poorly written (all LLM vendors seem to have an internal competition in writing confusing documentation). The specification glosses over or ignores important aspects of the protocol and provides no examples of conversation flow. In fact, it seems the entire website is not meant for reading the standard; instead, it pushes you toward tutorials on how to implement their SDKs. All example servers are implemented in Python or JavaScript, with the intention that you download and run them locally using stdio. Python and JavaScript are probably one of the worst choices of languages for something you want to work on anyone else's computer. The authors seem to realize this since all examples are available as Docker containers. Be honest... when was the last time you ran pip install and didn't end up in dependency hell? Am I being pretentious/judgmental in thinking that people in AI only really know Python, and the "well, it works on my computer" approach is still considered acceptable? This should be glaringly obvious to anyone that ever tried to run anything from Hugging Face. If you want to run MCP locally, wouldn't you prefer a portable language like Rust, Go, or even VM-based options such as Java or C#? The Problem When I started implementing the protocol, I immediately felt I had to reverse-engineer it. Important aspects of the SSE portion are missing from the documentation, and no one seemed to have implemented the "Streamable HTTP" yet; not even their own tooling like npx @modelcontextprotocol/inspector@latest. (To be fair, it might have been a skill issue on my part, pulling the wrong version, since it was available when I checked again a few weeks later. You can also find version at inspect.mcp.garden, which might be more convenient.) Once you grasp the architecture, you quickly realize that implementing an MCP server, or a client, could be a huge effort. The problem is that the SSE/Streamable HTTP implementations are trying to act like sockets, emulating stdio, without being one and is trying to do Everything Everywhere All at Once. HTTP+SSE Mode modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2024-11-05/basic/transports In HTTP+SSE mode, to achieve full duplex, the client sets up an SSE session to (e.g.) GET /sse for reads. The first read provides a URL where writes can be posted. The client then proceeds to use the given endpoint for writes, e.g., a request to POST /a-endpoint?session-id=1234. items.overview:
The article provides a detailed technical examination of MCP (Model Context Protocol), an open protocol designed to standardize how applications provide context to large language models (LLMs), with the goal of enabling LLMs to function as agents that can interact with various data sources and tools. MCP is positioned as a foundational standard for LLM-powered agent systems, with major industry players such as Anthropic (the main driver of MCP), IBM (with their competing Agent Communication Protocol, ACP), and Google (with Agent2Agent, A2A) all releasing their own protocols in this space. The rapid proliferation of MCP servers and clients—available at sites like mcp.so and pulsemcp.com—underscores the fast-moving nature of the ecosystem, but also brings to light significant concerns regarding engineering practices, documentation quality, and implementation guidance.

A core focus of the critique is MCP’s choice of transport protocols. MCP supports multiple transports, notably stdio (using stdin/stdout pipes for local communication) and HTTP-based approaches—specifically HTTP+SSE (Server-Sent Events) and a so-called "Streamable HTTP" mode, which attempts to provide bidirectional communication over REST semantics with SSE. The author notes that while stdio is straightforward and easy to reason about for local-first applications (such as IDE integrations), the HTTP+SSE and Streamable HTTP approaches introduce unnecessary complexity and corner cases, essentially re-implementing socket-like behavior without using established solutions like WebSockets. This design decision is further complicated by the lack of clear, comprehensive documentation and examples, particularly for the SSE/Streamable HTTP portions, making implementation challenging and error-prone. The author’s attempt to implement an MCP server in Go highlighted these issues, as official SDKs and tooling are primarily available in Python or JavaScript, and even these are often distributed as Docker containers to sidestep dependency issues.

The article’s significance lies in its practical, hands-on analysis of MCP’s technical and operational challenges, which are representative of broader issues in the AI tooling landscape: rapid protocol development, insufficient documentation, and immature engineering practices. For those interested in building reliable and ergonomic systems atop emerging LLM agent standards, understanding these pain points is crucial. The critique not only exposes the implementation difficulties and design trade-offs of MCP’s transport layer, but also points to opportunities for improvement—such as better SDKs, improved developer experience, or alternative transport mechanisms. Even for readers not directly adopting MCP, the insights provided are valuable for navigating the evolving LLM agent ecosystem and identifying areas where robust, user-friendly tooling is still needed.
items.context: MCP, or Model Context Protocol, is an emerging standard designed to facilitate communication between large language models (LLMs) and the applications or agent systems that use them. As LLMs become central to modern software, major tech companies like Anthropic, IBM, and Google are developing or adopting protocols like MCP to standardize how models are invoked, managed, and integrated into products. A key technical debate centers on MCP's choice of transport layer—specifically, its use of HTTP with Server-Sent Events (SSE) instead of alternatives like WebSockets or inter-process communication (IPC), which can impact performance, reliability, and developer experience. The rapid evolution of these protocols, often accompanied by sparse documentation and inconsistent engineering practices, creates challenges for developers aiming to build robust, user-friendly, and commercial-grade systems on top of LLM infrastructure. Understanding these issues is crucial for anyone interested in building or improving tools, SDKs, or platforms in the AI ecosystem.

narrative_raw:
# Today's Technical Digest: May 6, 2024

## CodeLLMs and Text-to-SQL Innovations

Two papers caught my eye today about the evolving landscape of AI code generation and database interaction.

The first paper on **benchmarking CodeLLMs and agents** reveals a significant imbalance in how we're evaluating these systems. While we're obsessively benchmarking code generation (60% of benchmarks!), we're almost completely ignoring requirements engineering (5%) and design phases (3%). This mirrors the industry's fixation on "code generation" rather than the full software development lifecycle. If we want AI to truly transform software engineering, we need to develop benchmarks that test the entire process, not just Python code synthesis.

The second paper, **HEXGEN-TEXT2SQL**, tackles a practical problem: how do you efficiently schedule and execute multi-stage LLM workflows for Text-to-SQL systems on GPU clusters? Their hierarchical scheduling approach claims impressive improvements - 1.41× faster latency and 1.65× better throughput compared to vLLM. This is the unglamorous but critical infrastructure work that will determine whether these LLM-based systems can actually perform in production environments. Worth investigating if you're building systems that require coordinating multiple LLM calls with interdependencies.

## DIY Hardware Hacking

The **PCB Strain Gauge** project is a delightful bit of hardware ingenuity. The creator built a strain gauge where the PCB itself is the sensing element, capable of measuring deflections in the micrometer range. This is a clever approach that simplifies construction while maintaining sensitivity. The project includes full manufacturing specs, assembly instructions, and even sample firmware. If you're into electronics or IoT sensing, this could be an elegant solution for mechanical sensing applications.

## Bioinformatics and Information Theory

The article on **DNA information content** is a fascinating exploration of information theory applied to biology. The author dives into the nuances of different definitions of "information" - storage space, Kolmogorov complexity, and Shannon information - and how each gives a different answer to the question "how much information is in DNA?"

What makes this piece exceptional is how it tackles the philosophical and mathematical challenges of quantifying biological information. The compression angle is particularly interesting - depending on your approach, human DNA might compress by either 25% or 99%, reflecting different notions of what constitutes "information." This piece rewards a full read, especially if you're interested in the intersection of information theory and biology.

## Software Engineering Improvements

The **Adaptive Hashing** article describes SBCL's (Steel Bank Common Lisp) approach to making hash tables both faster and more robust. Rather than using a single hash function, they adaptively switch between different hashing strategies based on the actual keys being stored. For EQ hash tables, they start with a constant hash function for small tables, then progressively upgrade to more sophisticated hash functions as needed. For EQUAL hash tables with composite keys, they initially hash only portions of the keys and expand as collisions increase.

This pragmatic approach balances performance in common cases with robustness against pathological inputs. The results show meaningful improvements in both aspects, and the technique could be applicable in other languages and systems.

## Protocol Design Critique

The critical analysis of **MCP (Model Context Protocol)** raises serious concerns about the design of this emerging standard for LLM/agent interaction. The author argues that the HTTP transport methods (HTTP+SSE and "Streamable HTTP") are fundamentally flawed attempts to reinvent WebSockets. They point out poor documentation, confusing specifications, and questionable design decisions that suggest the protocol was rushed without proper engineering rigor.

This is a must-read if you're considering implementing MCP. The critique is technical and substantive, not just complaining. The author makes a compelling case that the current approach should be reconsidered in favor of WebSockets for HTTP transport. Given that major players like IBM and Google are releasing competing standards (ACP and A2A), we may be heading toward a messy period of competing protocols before consolidation occurs.

---

These articles collectively highlight the rapid evolution of AI tools, infrastructure, and protocols, alongside clever hardware hacking and deep dives into information theory. The most concerning trend is the apparent rush to standardize agent protocols without sufficient engineering discipline, which could lead to significant technical debt as these systems mature.
